You Answer 8 Out of 10 Right. The Exam Still Beats You.

You remember the rule. You still lose marks. Then the exam throws "I am", "Let's", "Nobody", or "hardly" at you, and the marks disappear in half a second. Question tags don't beat you because you don't know the rule — they beat you because the exam is built entirely around the five exceptions nobody drills properly.

Quick Answer: A question tag repeats the main clause's auxiliary verb, reverses its polarity, and matches the subject with the correct pronoun. Five fixed forms — aren't I, shall we, didn't (for used to), isn't/aren't there, and they (for nobody/everybody/someone) — decide most tag questions in SSC CGL and Bank PO. Master the polarity rule plus these five exceptions and the topic stops costing marks.

Why Question Tags Keep Beating Strong Students

Here's the part nobody explains properly in a regular classroom: question tags aren't tested to check if you know the rule. They're tested to check if you can apply the rule under pressure, inside a sentence built specifically to hide the trap. Every wrong option in an SSC or Bank PO tag question is designed around one exact blind spot — and most aspirants walk straight into it because they were taught the rule in isolation, never against a real distractor sentence.

  • You apply the polarity rule correctly, but miss that "hardly", "never", or "seldom" already made the statement negative — so you flip the tag the wrong way.
  • You freeze on "I am" and default to "amn't I" or "isn't I", both of which are always wrong in standard exam English.
  • You keep the polarity the same after "Let's", because "shall we" doesn't feel like it "matches" anything you were taught to look for.
  • You match the verb correctly but use "he" or "she" for "nobody", "everybody", or "someone" instead of the required "they".
  • You second-guess a genuinely correct tag because it sounds unnatural compared to how it's said in spoken Indian English.

I know exactly how that feels — I've watched sharp students who ace tenses and articles stumble on this exact topic, purely because nobody showed them the fixed exceptions as a standalone checklist. But here's what most people get wrong: they keep collecting more example sentences instead of locking the small, fixed list that actually decides the outcome every single time.

5 Mistakes Aspirants Repeat Every Single Year

1. Matching polarity instead of reversing it.
A positive statement always needs a negative tag, and a negative statement always needs a positive one. Exams bury this rule inside long, distracting sentences so your eye catches the wrong cue before it reaches the comma.
Wrong: Your eldest sister lives in a big city, does she?
Correct: Your eldest sister lives in a big city, doesn't she?
SSC CGL Exam Pattern

2. Reaching for "isn't/wasn't" when no auxiliary is visible.
When the main clause is in simple present or simple past with no helping verb, the tag must use do/does/did — never isn't or wasn't, even if it "sounds" fine.
Wrong: Every Saturday, your mother prepares a pudding, isn't she?
Correct: Every Saturday, your mother prepares a pudding, doesn't she?
SSC CGL Exam Pattern

3. Defaulting to "isn't it" for every modal sentence.
The tag must repeat the exact modal used in the statement — should, could, would, must — never a generic "isn't it" thrown in because it sounds safe.
Wrong: It should be started early, isn't it?
Correct: It should be started early, shouldn't it?
Bank PO Exam Pattern

4. Inventing a tag for "I am".
Standard English has exactly one accepted tag for "I am", and it breaks the usual mirror-the-auxiliary pattern on purpose — students who try to "logic it out" almost always get it wrong.
Wrong: I am late, amn't I? / isn't I?
Correct: I am late, aren't I?

5. Guessing on "Let's" and indefinite pronouns.
"Let's" always takes "shall we", with no exceptions. Nobody, everybody, and someone always take "they" in the tag, regardless of the implied gender in the sentence.
Wrong: Let's start the meeting, will we? / Nobody came, did he?
Correct: Let's start the meeting, shall we? / Nobody came, did they?

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Matching polarity instead of reversing it

A positive statement must always take a negative tag.

Wrong: Your eldest sister lives in a big city, does she?

Correct: doesn't she?

❌
Mistake 2: Wrong auxiliary for simple present

Use does/doesn't when no helping verb is present in the clause.

Wrong: …prepares a pudding, isn't she?

Correct: doesn't she?

❌
Mistake 3: "isn't it" for every modal

The tag must repeat the exact modal used in the statement.

Wrong: …should be started early, isn't it?

Correct: shouldn't it?

❌
Mistake 4: "I am" tag

Only "aren't I" is accepted in standard exam English.

Wrong: I am late, amn't I?

Correct: aren't I?

❌
Mistake 5: "Let's" and "Nobody"

Let's → shall we; Nobody/everybody/someone → they.

Wrong: Let's go, will we? / Nobody came, did he?

Correct: shall we? / did they?

The 7-Step System for a Perfect Tag Every Time

You don't need twenty separate rules. You need one fixed sequence you can run through in under twenty seconds, every single time, regardless of how the exam disguises the sentence.

Step 1: Scan for hidden negatives first. Words like not, never, hardly, seldom, rarely, no one, and nobody already make the statement negative — even without the word "not" appearing anywhere near the tag position. If any of these is present, the tag must be positive.

❌ He never comes late, doesn't he?
✅ He never comes late, does he?

Step 2: Locate the auxiliary or modal in the main clause. is, are, was, were, have, has, had, will, would, can, could, should, must — repeat that exact word in the tag, unchanged except for polarity.

Step 3: If no auxiliary is visible, supply do/does/did. Match it to the tense and the person of the subject — never insert a helping verb the sentence didn't already imply.

❌ She writes novels, isn't she?
✅ She writes novels, doesn't she?

Step 4: Convert the subject to the correct pronoun. He/she/it stays as is; nouns become he/she/it/they based on number; nobody, everybody, anyone, and someone all become "they"; there stays as "there".

Step 5: Lock the five fixed exceptions cold. I am → aren't I. Let's → shall we. Used to → didn't. There is/are → isn't/aren't there. An imperative like "Open the door" → will you / won't you.

❌ He used to smoke, usedn't he?
✅ He used to smoke, didn't he?

Step 6: Never let the main verb slip into the tag. The tag is only auxiliary + pronoun + question mark — nothing else.

❌ He runs fast, doesn't he run?
✅ He runs fast, doesn't he?

Step 7: Re-read the whole sentence before locking your answer. A large share of wrong answers come from students who spot the first odd word and mark it, missing a genuine polarity error hiding later in the same sentence.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Scan for hidden negatives first

Never, hardly, seldom, nobody → the tag must be positive.

Example: He never comes late, does he?

2
Locate the auxiliary or modal

Repeat it exactly, only reversing polarity.

Example: It should be started early, shouldn't it?

3
Supply do/does/did when no auxiliary is visible

Match it to tense and person.

Example: She writes novels, doesn't she?

4
Convert the subject to the correct pronoun

Nobody/everybody/someone → they.

Example: Nobody came, did they?

5
Lock the five fixed exceptions

I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we; used to → didn't.

Example: I am ready, aren't I?

6
Never let the main verb slip into the tag

Only auxiliary + pronoun + question mark.

Example: He runs fast, doesn't he? (not doesn't he run)

7
Re-read the full sentence before answering

Don't lock onto the first odd word you spot.

How Rahul Went From 3 Wrong to Zero Wrong

Rahul, an SSC CGL aspirant from Pune, was losing two to three marks on nearly every mock test purely on question-tag questions — not because he didn't know the polarity rule, but because "I am", "Let's", and "nobody" kept catching him off guard under time pressure. For three weeks, he wrote only the five fixed exceptions on a single flashcard and reviewed it before every mock, without adding a single new example sentence. Tag-related errors in his mocks dropped to zero within that period. Nothing else in his preparation changed — just the shift from chasing endless examples to locking five fixed forms. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From 15+ Years of Coaching

  • Underline every negative word before you touch the tag. Hardly, never, seldom, rarely, no, and nobody decide the polarity before you even reach the comma.
  • Treat "I am" and "Let's" as fixed formulas, not calculations. The instant you see them, write "aren't I" or "shall we" automatically — don't reason it out mid-exam.
  • Practise only sentence formats that mirror real exam length. Short, textbook-style example sentences build false confidence; the actual exam always hides the tag inside a longer, more distracting clause.
  • Never trust how the sentence "sounds" in spoken Indian English. "Isn't it" gets used for everything in casual speech, but the exam accepts only the grammatically exact tag — your ear is not a reliable judge here.

The Bottom Line

Question tags stop costing marks the moment you stop treating them as twenty scattered rules and start running one fixed sequence: check for hidden negatives, find the auxiliary, match the pronoun, lock the five exceptions, keep the main verb out, and re-read before you answer. That sequence, paired with the five fixed forms, turns question tags from a guessing game into one of the most reliable, predictable mark-scoring sections in SSC CGL and Bank PO.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the most common question tag error in SSC CGL?

A: Using the same polarity as the statement, and using "isn't/wasn't" instead of do/does/did when no auxiliary is present in the main clause.

Q: Is "aren't I" the only correct tag for "I am"?

A: Yes. "Amn't I" and "isn't I" are always wrong in standard exam English; "aren't I" is the only accepted fixed form.

Q: What tag is used after "Let's"?

A: Always "shall we". "Will we" or "won't we" is incorrect after "Let's" in every case.

Q: Do words like "hardly" and "never" change the tag?

A: Yes. They make the statement negative on their own, so the tag that follows must be positive.

Q: Is this eBook useful if I already know basic question tag rules?

A: Yes. Most aspirants already know the basic rule; what costs marks is the five fixed exceptions and hidden-negative sentences, which this book focuses on specifically.

Q: Will these rules work for IBPS PO as well?

A: Yes. Question-tag patterns overlap heavily across SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB and similar competitive exams.

Q: How is "there is/are" handled in a question tag?

A: "There" is treated as the subject and repeated in the tag as "isn't there" or "aren't there", matching the singular or plural form used in the statement.

Q: Why do imperative sentences take "will you" as a tag?

A: Imperative sentences (commands or requests) don't have a visible subject or auxiliary, so English grammar assigns them the fixed tag "will you" or "won't you" by convention.
